entities.name: Lombard Kingdom
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Lombard Kingdom (568–774 CE), established when the Germanic Lombards (Langobards — 'Long Beards') under King Alboin crossed the Alps into Italy, controlled the Po Valley and much of Italy for 206 years before Charlemagne's conquest — leaving permanent marks on Italian place names (Lombardy, Langobard), law (Lombard law codes), and the political fragmentation of Italy that persisted until 1861. The Lombard invasion of 568 permanently destroyed the remnants of Roman Italy that Justinian had just reconquered, ending Byzantine authority over northern Italy.

Alboin's Lombards, who had just defeated and absorbed the Gepids in Pannonia (using Gepid skulls as drinking cups, according to Paul the Deacon), entered an Italy exhausted by 20 years of Byzantine-Ostrogothic war (535-554). The Lombards established capitals at Pavia (royal residence) and Cividale del Friuli (first capital). Their law code — the Edictum Rothari (643 CE), the first Germanic law code in Italy — codified customary Lombard law in Latin, creating an early medieval legal tradition.

The Lombard kingdom was fiercely independent: it controlled northern Italy (Langobardia Maior) while separate Lombard duchies in Spoleto and Benevento (Langobardia Minor) controlled central and southern Italy. Pope Gregory I's appeals to the Franks for protection against the Lombards established the pattern of papal-Frankish alliance that led to Charlemagne's 774 conquest and the creation of the Papal States — the political foundation of medieval Western Christendom. Italy's north-south divide can be traced in part to this Lombard-Byzantine split.
